High-quality studies should therefore pre-specify the clinical question, define reference standards and adjudication procedures, separate patients rather than images across data partitions, avoid leakage from longitudinal records, and distinguish development from external validation cohorts.

Established reporting frameworks, including the Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM) and the CONSORT-AI extension for clinical trials, provide useful foundations for transparent evaluation [10, 11].

Future studies should demonstrate incremental value over strong unimodal and clinical baselines, address missing data and distribution shifts, and validate performance across institutions, devices, and diverse patient populations.
Models should also be evaluated for their capacity to complement, rather than merely replicate, clinician judgement.

Evaluation should extend beyond retrospective discrimination metrics to outcomes relevant to patients and health systems, including visual function, referral appropriateness, time to treatment, treatment burden, safety, access, and patient experience.
These observations reinforce the need for independent external validation, prospective assessment where feasible, subgroup analyses and transparent characterization of the intended-use population.

Report transparently how missing modalities are handled and which data are available at the point of use.
Perform task-specific validation, calibration, uncertainty assessment, and failure-mode evaluation of foundation models before clinical workflow use.
